_readme: OKLAHOMA CIVIL DEADLINE RULES -- 9 rows, 12 O.S. §§ 2006, 2012, 3233,
3234 and 3236. Statutory civil procedure: the Oklahoma Pleading Code,
Title 12, so the computation rule is a STATUTE and not a court rule.
== TWO FACTS ABOUT WHAT A PARTY DID, AND BOTH RUN LATE IF DEFAULTED =====
READ THIS BEFORE ADDING ANY ANSWER ROW. Oklahoma's answer period depends
on two things the engine has no field for, and each is seeded as its own
row with an unmissable trigger name rather than defaulted.
(1) THE PLAINTIFF'S ELECTION -- 20 OR 35 DAYS. § 2012(A)(4): `The party
requesting a summons to be issued or filing a counter-claim or
cross-claim MAY ELECT to have the answer served within thirty-five (35)
days IN LIEU OF the twenty (20) days set forth in this section.` That is
a choice the REQUESTING party made, recorded on the summons, not
derivable from any date. Same shape as Louisiana's art. 1001. GUESSING
35 WHERE 20 APPLIES COMPUTES FIFTEEN DAYS LATE.
(2) THE MAIL-SERVICE PROVISO IS A DIFFERENT TRIGGER, NOT A DIFFERENT
AMOUNT. § 2006(D) ends: `provided, however, when a summons and petition
are served by mail, a defendant shall serve an answer within twenty (20)
days or thirty-five (35) days if pursuant to subsection A of Section 2012
of this title, AFTER THE DATE OF RECEIPT OR IF REFUSED, THE DATE OF
REFUSAL of the summons and petition by the defendant.` So on mailed
process the clock runs from RECEIPT (or refusal), not from service, and
takes NO three-day extension. A caller who supplied a service date to the
ordinary row instead would compute EARLY.
Four answer rows result, and the trigger names say which is which. Do not
collapse them.
== THE SIX CARVED-OUT SECTIONS -- RECORD, DO NOT INHERIT ================
§ 2006(A)(1): `EXCEPT FOR THE TIMES PROVIDED IN SECTIONS 765, 990.3,
1148.4, 1148.5, 1148.5A, AND 1756 OF THIS TITLE, when the period of time
prescribed or allowed is less than eleven (11) days, intermediate legal
holidays ... shall be excluded from the computation.`
An ENUMERATED opt-out -- narrower and more tractable than Louisiana's
open-ended `expressly excluded` and Minnesota's open-ended opt-in, but a
standard-level flag still cannot express it. NONE OF THE SIX IS IN THIS
BATCH, so the constraint is recordable rather than blocking. SEEDING A
ROW UNDER ANY OF THEM LATER WITHOUT NOTICING WOULD SILENTLY APPLY AN
EXCLUSION THE STATUTE REMOVES, computing LATE. None of the six was read;
only the carve-out was noted.
== THE WEEKEND QUESTION -- LOUISIANA'S SHAPE, SAVED BY ONE CLAUSE =======
§ 2006(A)(1) rolls the last day only if it `is a legal holiday as defined
by Section 82.1 of Title 25 ... or any other day when the office of the
court clerk does not remain open`. SATURDAY AND SUNDAY ARE NOT NAMED --
exactly the structure that BLOCKED Louisiana one gate earlier.
Oklahoma resolves it in the first eight words of its holiday statute.
25 O.S. § 82.1(A): `The designation and dates of holidays in Oklahoma
shall be as follows: EACH SATURDAY, SUNDAY, New Year's Day ...`. Both
weekend days are statutory holidays, STATEWIDE, with no county or parish
qualification. So isWeekend() is correct for Oklahoma -- by a different
textual route than any common-law state, and only because of a statute
the computation rule points at rather than anything in the rule itself.
ok_12_2006 declares short_period_exclusion_days: 11, joining Tennessee,
Arizona, Wisconsin and Alabama. Six seeded states use 7; Minnesota, Utah
and Nevada have none. Copying a neighbour's 7 would count intermediate
days on periods of 7-10 that Oklahoma excludes, computing EARLY.
== THE CALENDAR IS MISSING ONE DAY A YEAR, DISCLOSED ====================
sql/sairnlaw_deadline_calendars_oklahoma.json, 2026-2031, generated by
tools/gen_ok_calendar.py. § 82.1(A) gives `the day before OR after
Christmas if Christmas is not on a Saturday or Sunday` and DOES NOT SAY
WHICH; § 82.1(B) makes the Governor's annual Executive Order the only
thing that resolves it.
THE ORDERS ARE REACHABLE AND UNREADABLE. sos.ok.gov publishes them and
they are identifiable by title -- EO 2026-26 AMENDED, 15 July 2026, `the
following dates be observed as holidays by the State of Oklahoma in 2027`
-- but every one is a SINGLE-PAGE SCANNED IMAGE with zero extractable
text. Reading the dates needs OCR, which this project does not treat as a
verbatim source. So the day is OMITTED, which reports EARLY and is safe;
guessing would add a non-holiday (LATE) and still miss the real one.
THREE THINGS THE CALENDAR DOES NOT HAVE, all asserted by the generator:
NO JUNETEENTH (§ 2006 points at § 82.1 alone; Oklahoma's is the THIRD
SATURDAY in June under § 82.4, already a non-day, and encoding 19 June
would add a holiday Oklahoma does not have); NO COLUMBUS DAY; and none of
§ 82.2's commemorative days, which was READ to confirm it rather than
assumed. THE DAY AFTER THANKSGIVING *IS* a statutory holiday here.
§ 2006(D) adds three days for MAIL, THIRD-PARTY COMMERCIAL CARRIER or
ELECTRONIC MEANS, added TO THE PRESCRIBED PERIOD. Electronic qualifies,
as in Oregon and Massachusetts and unlike Nevada, West Virginia, New York
and the federal rule. OKLAHOMA IS THE ONLY SEEDED JURISDICTION NAMING
THIRD-PARTY COMMERCIAL CARRIER as its own category -- Texas lists
commercial delivery among its service methods but extends for mail alone,
so the two must not be read across.
The extension attaches to the rows that run after service of a paper
between parties. It does NOT attach to the four answer rows: the ordinary
20/35-day rows run from service of the summons and petition, which is
process, and the two receipt/refusal rows are the proviso that replaces
the extension rather than taking it.
== WHAT IS DELIBERATELY NOT SEEDED =====================================
(1) THE RESERVATION OF TIME. § 2012(A)(1)(b): a defendant `may file a
reservation of time which shall extend the time to respond twenty
(20) days from the last date for answering`, and filing it WAIVES the
defences in § 2012(B)(2)-(6) and (9). A filing the engine cannot see;
it only ever extends, so omitting it reports EARLY.
(2) Any BACKWARD row -- § 2006 has no backward provision, so
rollover_suffix_backward is blank.
(3) Appellate rows.
the carve-out above.
== NOT MODELLED, ALL EARLY, DISCLOSED ==================================
§ 2006(A)(1)'s clerk-closure limb is a PARTIAL-closure test -- a day when
the office `does not remain open for public business until the regularly
scheduled closing time` -- broader than a simple closed/open test, and it
appears in BOTH the rollover and the 11-day exclusion. It is ADDITIONAL
to the holiday list rather than a replacement, so omitting it reports
EARLY. § 82.1(B)'s presidential-national-holiday limb, which the Governor
MAY adopt, is ad hoc. § 2012(A)(3) and (5) carry `unless the order
otherwise directs` / `unless a different time is fixed by order of the
court`, and § 3236 `or within such shorter or longer time as the court
may allow` -- court orders the engine cannot see.
§ 2004 (process and how service is made) was not read, so what date a
caller supplies for `service of the summons and petition` is not sourced
from the statute text. The receipt/refusal rows are safer in this respect:
the proviso names the operative event itself.

rules.label: Answer within 20 days after service of the summons and petition (Oklahoma) — the DEFAULT election

authority.quote: Unless a different time is prescribed by law, a defendant shall serve an answer: a. within twenty (20) days after the service of the summons and petition upon the defendant,
authority.note: TWENTY DAYS, AND THE TRIGGER NAME CARRIES THE ELECTION ON PURPOSE. § 2012(A)(4) lets the party requesting the summons ELECT thirty-five days in lieu of twenty, and that choice is a fact about what the plaintiff did — recorded on the summons, not derivable from any date. Two rows, never one with a default: guessing 35 where 20 applies computes FIFTEEN DAYS LATE. THIS ROW IS FOR SERVICE OTHER THAN BY MAIL. Where the summons and petition were served BY MAIL, § 2006(D)'s proviso replaces this trigger entirely — the clock runs from the date of RECEIPT, or of REFUSAL — and there is a separate row for it. NO SERVICE EXTENSION: the period runs from service of PROCESS, and § 2006(D)'s three days reach a 'notice or other paper', with the proviso carving mailed process out expressly. § 2004 (how service is made) was not read, so what a caller supplies as the service date is not sourced here.

rules.label: Answer within 35 days — where the requesting party ELECTED the longer period (Oklahoma)

authority.quote: The party requesting a summons to be issued or filing a counter-claim or cross-claim may elect to have the answer served within thirty-five (35) days in lieu of the twenty (20) days set forth in this section.
authority.note: THIRTY-FIVE DAYS, AND ONLY WHERE THE ELECTION WAS ACTUALLY MADE. This is not an alternative the defendant chooses or the engine infers — it is the REQUESTING party's election, and it appears on the summons. Use this row only when the summons says so. The election also reaches a counterclaim or crossclaim, so it is available on those pleadings too, but no separate 35-day crossclaim row is seeded because the trigger would be indistinguishable from this one without a party-role field. IF IN DOUBT USE THE 20-DAY ROW: it computes EARLY, which is safe, where this one computes FIFTEEN DAYS LATE if the election was never made. NO SERVICE EXTENSION, for the same reason as the 20-day row.

rules.label: Answer within 20 days after RECEIPT or REFUSAL — summons and petition served by mail (Oklahoma)

authority.quote: provided, however, when a summons and petition are served by mail, a defendant shall serve an answer within twenty (20) days or thirty-five (35) days if pursuant to subsection A of Section 2012 of this title, after the date of receipt or if refused, the date of refusal of the summons and petition by the defendant.
authority.note: THE PROVISO IS A DIFFERENT TRIGGER, NOT A DIFFERENT AMOUNT — which is why it is its own row rather than a service_extension on the ordinary answer row. On mailed process the twenty days run from THE DATE OF RECEIPT, or if the defendant refused it, THE DATE OF REFUSAL. Not from service, and NOT from service plus three: the proviso REPLACES § 2006(D)'s three-day extension for this situation rather than stacking with it. Supply the receipt or refusal date. A caller who supplied the mailing date to the ordinary § 2012(A)(1) row instead would compute EARLY. Refusal is treated identically to receipt by the statute, so one trigger covers both and the row does not need to know which happened. The 35-day variant of the same proviso is a separate row.

rules.label: Answer within 35 days after RECEIPT or REFUSAL — mailed process AND the 35-day election (Oklahoma)

authority.quote: provided, however, when a summons and petition are served by mail, a defendant shall serve an answer within twenty (20) days or thirty-five (35) days if pursuant to subsection A of Section 2012 of this title, after the date of receipt or if refused, the date of refusal of the summons and petition by the defendant.
authority.note: THE ROW WHERE BOTH FACTS APPLY AT ONCE: the summons and petition were served BY MAIL, and the requesting party ELECTED thirty-five days under § 2012(A). Seeded separately because the engine cannot derive either fact, and combining them into a default would compound two guesses. Runs from RECEIPT or REFUSAL like its 20-day sibling. IF EITHER FACT IS UNCERTAIN, PREFER THE SHORTER ROW — a shorter period computes EARLY, which is safe; this one is fifteen days LATE if the election was never made. NO SERVICE EXTENSION: the proviso replaces it.

authority.quote: A party served with a pleading stating a cross-claim against that party shall serve an answer thereto within twenty (20) days after the service upon the party.
authority.note: TWENTY DAYS. THE SERVICE EXTENSION APPLIES HERE and not on the answer-to-petition rows: a pleading stating a crossclaim is a paper served between parties, which is what § 2006(D) reaches, where the summons and petition are process. Note § 2012(A)(4)'s election also reaches a party 'filing a counter-claim or cross-claim', so a 35-day crossclaim is possible in principle — no row is seeded for it because its trigger would be indistinguishable from this one without a field for who elected what, and the 20-day row computes EARLY, which is the safe direction.

service_extension.note: § 2006(D): three days for mail, THIRD-PARTY COMMERCIAL CARRIER or electronic means, added TO THE PRESCRIBED PERIOD. Electronic qualifies, unlike Nevada, West Virginia, New York and the federal rule. Oklahoma is the ONLY seeded jurisdiction naming third-party commercial carrier as its own category — Texas lists commercial delivery among its methods but extends for mail alone, so do not read the two across.

rules.label: Reply to a counterclaim in the answer (Oklahoma)

authority.quote: The plaintiff shall serve a reply to a counterclaim in the answer within twenty (20) days after service of the answer or, if a reply is ordered by the court, within twenty (20) days after service of the order, unless the order otherwise directs.
authority.note: TWENTY DAYS FROM SERVICE OF THE ANSWER that contains the counterclaim. The sentence carries a SECOND limb — twenty days after service of a court ORDER where a reply is ordered — which is not seeded as its own row because it is reachable only when such an order exists and the row would then be indistinguishable by trigger date alone; a caller in that position should supply the order's service date to this row and read the citation. 'Unless the order otherwise directs' is an override the engine cannot see. The extension applies: an answer is a paper served between parties.

authority.quote: The party upon whom the interrogatories have been served shall serve a copy of the answers, and objections if any, within thirty (30) days after the service of the interrogatories.
authority.note: THIRTY DAYS, matching § 3234 exactly. NO DEFENDANT FLOOR: §§ 3233 and 3234 were searched for 'shall not be required', 'before the expiration', 'after service of the summons' and 'commencement of the action' and returned ZERO hits each, so unlike Ohio, Indiana, Georgia, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Missouri, North Carolina, Virginia, Oregon and Arkansas there is no later-of sibling row. Reported as a searched-for absence, not an assumption. § 3236 is the exception and has its own shape — see that row.

rules.label: Response to a request for production or inspection (Oklahoma)

authority.quote: The party to whom the request is directed shall respond in writing within thirty (30) days after being served.
authority.note: THIRTY DAYS. NO DEFENDANT FLOOR (searched; see the § 3233 row). This is the deadline for the written RESPONSE, not for the production itself.

rules.label: Response to requests for admission (Oklahoma) — the period does NOT start until an answer to the petition is filed; SILENCE ADMITS

authority.quote: The matter is admitted unless, within thirty (30) days after service of the request, or within such shorter or longer time as the court may allow, the party to whom the request is directed serves upon the party requesting the admission a written answer or objection addressed to the matter, signed by the party or by the party's attorney. The thirty-day response period shall not commence until an answer to the petition is filed.
authority.note: THIRTY DAYS, BUT THE PERIOD DOES NOT COMMENCE UNTIL AN ANSWER TO THE PETITION IS FILED — a sentence no other seeded admissions rule has, and the reason this is a later_of rather than a plain row. The clock runs thirty days from the LATER of service of the request and the filing of the answer, so BOTH DATES ARE REQUIRED and the engine refuses on a partial set. This is a plain `resolve: later_of` on trigger DATES sharing ONE count, not the `resolve_periods` shape Oregon and Georgia need, because there is only one number here. SEEDING IT AS A FLAT 30-DAY ROW WOULD COMPUTE EARLY whenever the answer had not yet been filed. MISSING IT ADMITS THE MATTER — the rule is phrased as 'the matter is admitted unless'. Unlike Oregon and Missouri, Oklahoma requires NO warning on the face of the request, so nothing on the document alerts the recipient. The same sentence continues with an exception not modelled: 'upon leave of court or otherwise agreed to in writing by the parties subject to Section 3229 of this title, the response to the request may be required prior to the filing of an answer' — a court order or written agreement the engine cannot see, which would make the true deadline EARLIER than this row's, so a caller who knows of one must not rely on this date. NO SERVICE EXTENSION: no seeded rule combines a multi-trigger resolution with one, the engine has never been exercised on that combination, and the interaction is not settled by any statute text.
